Q: Java Mocking Issue When Using Parallel Streams A:

Easiest way to solve it is moving ImageIO.read to a separate service and mocking it.

I suspect that the problem is caused by the fact that Thread used by parallelStream has its own class loader. mockStatic does its magic by switching classloaders and is unable to do it for a thread it doesn't know about.

Another solution is to mock parallelStream to work in the same thread, but you will probably open another can of worms by that.

Q: Can't install onnxruntime A:

This is because of the versioning issue with various dependencies, Just follow these steps you should be fine.

Use Conda for environments https://conda-forge.org/download/

conda create -n crewenv python=3.11.10
conda activate crewenv

Install crewai and dependencies

pip install crewai==0.80.0
pip install socksio

Create Crewai boilerplate

crewai create crew newAgent
cd newAgent
crewai install

If it shows Error, copy these dependencies to the pyproject.toml file

"dependencies = [
   "crewai[tools]>=0.80.0,<1.0.0",
   "onnxruntime==1.15.0",
   "socksio>=1.0.0",
   "pyarrow==17.0.0",
]"

then

pip install .
crewai install
crewai run

working boilerplate can be found on my repo below https://github.com/IgnatiusAndrew/crewai-boilerplate

you should be fine to go, Let me know if the issue persists

Q: Jenkins Pipeline docker.withRegistry() push leads to endless loop A:

You would need to check if the issue persists with Jenkins Docker commons 1.21

The PR 86 "docker login - get password from stdin" was reverted (PR 108).
And it includes JENKINS-69436 "Error: cannot perform an interactive login from a non TTY device".

That means the docker.withRegistry step has better chances now (since Aug. 2022 and docker commons 1.21) to execute successfully.

Q: apache Access Control Allow Origin issue A:

For us this worked only from the same domain. We are trying to add the Origin in the header Access-Control-Allow-Origin in the BE depending if is allowed in a list of allowed origin addresses. But we have issues with Apache right now, because it adds this header with value * all the time.

That is because of Apache config line:

Header set Access-Control-Allow-Origin "*"

We try to see if we can execute this only on some of the requests.

Q: How do I generate a random integer in C#? A:

Note for .NET Core and Modern .NET

Creating multiple Random instances is less likely to produce identical sequences in .NET Core than it was in older .NET Framework versions.

Historically, Random() used Environment.TickCount as its default seed. Consequently, instances created in quick succession could receive the same seed and produce identical sequences.

In .NET Core 2.0, the implementation was changed to initialize the seed using:

Guid.NewGuid().GetHashCode()

See the relevant change here:

  • CoreCLR pull request and diff
  • Related discussion: Did Microsoft change Random's default seed?

This substantially reduced the likelihood that two instances created close together would produce the same sequence.

Update

The GUID-based implementation was later replaced. The seed is now initialized using random bytes internally:

Interop.GetRandomBytes((byte*)&result, sizeof(int));

The exact implementation varies by .NET version. In modern .NET, prefer reusing:

Random.Shared

For example:

int value = Random.Shared.Next();

Random is still not cryptographically secure. For security-sensitive values, use the APIs in System.Security.Cryptography, such as:

int value = RandomNumberGenerator.GetInt32(maxValue);

Q: How to unnest a list-column as new rows in pre-existing columns? A:

The solutions below are 2 orders of magnitude faster and needs much less memory.

original <- function() {
  purrr::map(
    .x = split(ex, ~rownames(ex)),
    .f = \(df) {
      df_to_add = unnest(df[, "z"], z)
      dplyr::select(df, x, y) |> 
        bind_rows(df_to_add)
    }
  ) |> 
    bind_rows() |> 
    select(-z) |> 
    drop_na()
}

rui1 <- function() bind_rows(ex[-3], do.call(rbind, ex[[3]])) |> drop_na()
rui2 <- function() rbind(ex[-3], do.call(rbind, ex[[3]])) |> na.omit()

bench::mark(original(), rui1(), rui2(), col(), check = FALSE)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 6
#>   expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
#>   <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
#> 1 original()   14.5ms   15.3ms      62.1    1.99MB     9.55
#> 2 rui1()      314.9µs  353.8µs    2590.    47.66KB     8.43
#> 3 rui2()      201.2µs    238µs    3712.    26.06KB    10.4 

library(microbenchmark)
microbenchmark(original(), rui1(), rui2()) |> print(order = "median")
#> Unit: microseconds
#>        expr     min       lq      mean   median       uq     max neval cld
#>      rui2()   224.5   275.40   325.794   306.30   346.75   683.5   100   b
#>      rui1()   334.9   363.35   465.796   398.15   462.80  3173.3   100   b
#>  original() 13254.1 14440.80 16645.104 14879.60 17207.40 66733.8   100  a

Created on 2026-07-21 with reprex v2.1.1

When run outside reprex I get much less memory use, rui1 only 216B and rui2 0B.

I also tried timing with bigger data and the results were comparable to the results above. For instance, with a data set with 5000+ rows.

ex_backup <- ex
for(i in 1:10) ex <- rbind(ex, ex)
dim(ex)
#> [1] 5120    3
